C005.subject: globalization
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: globalization within-country income inequality]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data analysis of income Gini coefficients and trade flows between developed and low-wage economies (e.g., from World Bank, OECD, or WIOD) for countries with varying redistributive institutions (e.g., tax/transfer systems) — Directly tests the qualified hypothesis by comparing inequality changes in developed economies with and without strong redistributive institutions, isolating the effect of trade liberalization with low-wage partners through econometric controls.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of studies on trade liberalization and wage dispersion (e.g., survey articles in Journal of Economic Literature or World Development), focusing on developed economy results post-1990 — Synthesizes existing empirical evidence to determine the overall direction and magnitude of the effect, clarifying whether the disputed hypothesis holds across different methodologies and time periods.

qualifier.condition: when focusing on trade liberalization with low-wage economies and without strong redistributive institutions

C006.subject: globalization
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: globalization within-country income inequality]

[PATH:empirical] World Development Indicators (WDI) panel data on trade openness and Gini coefficients for OECD countries (1990-2020), controlling for technology and education — Provides cross-country time-series evidence to test the direct causal effect of globalization (measured as trade/GDP ratio or FDI flows) on within-country income inequality in developed economies, with controls for confounding factors.

[PATH:literature] Milanovic, B. (2016). Global Inequality: A New Approach for the Age of Globalization. Harvard University Press. — Summarizes and critiques empirical findings on how globalization affects inequality, including the Kuznets-wave hypothesis and the role of skill-biased technical change, offering a balanced synthesis of the disputed hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of trade and inequality (e.g., Stolper-Samuelson theorem, Melitz-type heterogeneous firm models) applied to developed economies — Evaluates whether predictions about rising within-country inequality from comparative advantage and firm heterogeneity hold under modern trade patterns (e.g., offshoring, service trade), helping to identify mechanisms and boundary conditions.

C007.subject: globalization
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: globalization within-country income inequality]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data analysis of trade openness, government education spending, and Gini coefficients across developing economies (e.g., World Bank World Development Indicators and UNESCO education expenditure data, 1990-2020) — Directly tests the conditional hypothesis by measuring how the interaction between globalization (trade/GDP ratio) and public education investment affects within-country income inequality, controlling for other factors like FDI and institutional quality.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of countries like South Korea, Brazil, and Vietnam that experienced rapid globalization with varying levels of education/skills investment, using household survey data (e.g., LIS, SEDLAC) to trace inequality trends — Provides qualitative and quantitative depth to identify whether heavy education investment mitigates or reverses the inequality effects of globalization, addressing causal mechanisms and context-specific conditions.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing econometric studies on globalization and inequality, focusing on moderator variables such as education spending and skill-upgrading policies (e.g., reviews in Journal of International Economics or World Development) — Synthesizes accumulated evidence to assess the robustness of the conditional effect across different samples, methods, and time periods, highlighting gaps and convergence in findings.

qualifier.condition: when governments invest heavily in education and skills training for low-income workers

C008.subject: globalization
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: globalization within-country income inequality]

[PATH:empirical] World Bank World Development Indicators (WDI) and Standardized World Income Inequality Database (SWIID) panel data for developing economies (1990-2020) — Directly tests the hypothesis by correlating trade openness / FDI inflows (proxies for globalization) with Gini coefficients across countries and time, controlling for structural factors.

[PATH:literature] Dorn, D., & Levell, P. (2021). 'Trade and Inequality in Developing Countries: A Review of the Evidence.' Journal of Economic Literature. — Provides a systematic review of empirical studies on this disputed relationship, highlighting methodological disagreements and context-dependent results.

[PATH:theoretical] Stolper-Samuelson theorem with extensions for heterogeneous firms and skill-biased technical change (theoretical modeling) — Derives predictions under different assumptions (e.g., factor endowments, labor mobility) to explain why globalization may increase or decrease inequality in developing economies, informing targeted empirical tests.

C009.subject: globalization's effect on income inequality
C009.object: domestic institutional quality falls below a threshold of rule-of-law index 0.4
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: globalization's effect on income inequality domestic institutional quality falls below a threshold of rule-of-law index 0.4]

[PATH:empirical] World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI) Rule of Law index merged with World Inequality Database (WID) on income inequality for developing economies, panel regression with threshold effects — Directly tests the hypothesized threshold of 0.4 rule-of-law index by estimating non-linear or threshold regression models that allow the effect of globalization (trade/GDP, FDI inflows) on inequality to vary with institutional quality, explicitly identifying reversal point.

[PATH:theoretical] Rodrik, D. (1998). 'Why Do More Open Economies Have Bigger Governments?' Journal of Political Economy, or Acemoglu, D., Johnson, S., & Robinson, J. A. (2001). 'The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development' — Provides theoretical frameworks linking weak institutions to distributional consequences of globalization. Rodrik's work on compensation hypothesis and Acemoglu et al. on institutional persistence offer mechanisms for why low rule-of-law might reverse globalization's inequality effects, supporting or challenging the causal logic behind the threshold.

[PATH:literature] Systematic meta-analysis of 50+ empirical studies on globalization-inequality nexus in developing countries (e.g., from Journal of International Economics, World Development), focusing on studies that include interaction terms with governance or rule-of-law indices — A meta-analysis can synthesize existing evidence for a threshold effect, identify consistent patterns across different countries and time periods, and assess whether the 0.4 rule-of-law boundary appears robustly in the literature or is an artifact of specific data or methods.

qualifier.context: below this threshold, globalization increases rather than decreases income inequality, regardless of trade openness

C010.subject: globalization’s effect on income inequality
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: globalization’s effect on income inequality domestic institutional quality]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data regression of Gini coefficients on trade openness, financial globalization indices, and institutional quality (e.g., World Governance Indicators) for OECD countries from 1990 to present, with interaction terms. — Directly tests whether the effect of globalization on income inequality varies significantly with domestic institutional quality, controlling for time and country fixed effects.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on globalization and inequality in OECD countries, stratified by institutional quality quartiles. — Synthesizes evidence across multiple contexts to assess whether results are invariant or heterogeneous, providing a robust check on the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models incorporating endogenous institutional responses to globalization (e.g., Acemoglu & Robinson-type frameworks) to derive predictions about inequality dynamics under varying institutional constraints. — Clarifies causal mechanisms and boundary conditions, helping to evaluate whether invariance is theoretically plausible or depends on specific institutional features.
